newsitem.title: FRANCE: Oil and debt change give Algeria breathing space.
newsitem.headline: Oil and debt change give Algeria breathing space.

text.p: Higher oil prices, kept up by the U.S.-Iraq standoff, and debt rescheduling are giving Algeria an economic bonus to try to end years of violence, diplomats and analysts said on Wednesday.
Each extra dollar per barrel of oil means another $500 million per year income for Algeria.
But economic reform efforts, population growth, politics and Moslem fundamentalism in the southern mediterranean country have drawn an uncertain political map.

There are encouraging signs -- a rise of 5.2 percent last year in gross domestic product and 4.4 percent in the first half of 1996. On Wednesday, the cabinet said inflation had been cut to 19.3 percent in the year to last July from 30 percent in the previous period.
But the security situation is still bad and unemployment a threat, say diplomats.

"It is a race against growing despair in a growing army of young jobless that is by no means certain to be won," one diplomat said, pointing out that two-thirds of the 29 million population was under 30 years and formed 60 percent of jobless.

OPEC-member Algeria, rocked by poverty riots in 1988 and thrown in turmoil by massive support for Islamic fundamentalism from young people seeking an antidote to apparent political indifference, is struggling to switch to a free market.

In a workforce of around 5.4 million, some 400 state-run firms outside an efficient energy sector provide jobs for around 1.7 million which the authorities believe are essential to protect. It already has 2.1 million unemployed.
Algeria has won praise from the International Monetary Fund for cutting subsidies on essentials like bread and milk but fuelled local despair as inflation hovers around 20 percent.
Official figures forecast the population rising to 31 million in four years and 35 million by 2005.

"Hydrocarbons are the bright spot. They are producing and will continue to produce even more but that does not help unemployment. Heavy industry is overmanned, inefficient and producing expensive goods no-one wants," the diplomat added.
"Economic problems will continue. With energy earnings, the government will be able to keep a social security net. But people are fed up at not being able to lead a normal life."
The government has been working to create jobs but figures this week showed central and local government created only 35,000 and housing and public work about 10,000 in 1995.
Farming provided another 67,000 but outside the energy sector, industry lost about 9,000 jobs while applications for work through a state agency soared.

Efforts to get foreign investment have had some success, but almost entirely in the oil and gas fields. Algeria has signed over 30 contracts in the past 10 years with foreign oil companies involving billions of dollars.
Britain's British Petroleum signed a 3.5 billion deal for gas exploration which, if successful, will need a 500 km (310 mile) pipeline in the Sahara.

In November, a new Maghreb pipeline is due to come on stream, pumping 9.5 billion cubic metres of gas to Spain, Portugal and Morocco. present gas exports total 30 billion cubic metres and Algeria plans to double this by early next century.
One economic analyst said: "You are looking at early next century for earnings from these, and meanwhile debt repayments are going to start weighing heavily again from 1997-98."
Algeria rescheduled more than 12 billion in government debt in 1994 and 1995 and over 2 billion in commercial debt this year.
"That took repayments from nearly 100 percent of foreign income in the peak early in 1994 to around 34 percent, but it will start growing again next year," the analyst said.
